source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on the Rediscovery of Scientific Insights
finding: Agents get only the research question of a published empirical paper and must redo the study. Scored against the paper's claims. Even the best agent rediscovers under half.
numbers: 30 core tasks, 3 runs each. Claude Code (Sonnet-4) F1 46.7; Codex gpt-5-medium 41.9; OpenHands gpt-5 37.9; OpenHands o4-mini 31.9. Median coefficient of variation across tasks 0.37 even for the best agent, over 0.6 for weaker ones.
quote: even the strongest agents achieve limited rediscovery success (<50 F1), exhibit high variance across runs
limits: Tasks are recent ML-behaviour papers, not historical science. Lightweight experiments only.
agent_relevance: A case treated as a re-doable study is hard for agents. One run of a case is not evidence; need repeats and a variance report.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench, failure analysis
finding: Failures are mostly in research planning and in going from evidence to conclusion, especially designing proper controls, not in coding. Scores are high where the procedure is fixed and low where the agent must design controls.
numbers: Best-task F1: Lost in the Middle 91.7, Persona with Catch 88.6, CoT Without Prompting 82.6. Same task can differ by 56 F1 between agents (Claude Code 82.6 vs OpenHands gpt-5 26.4).
limits: Failure categories assigned by the authors' judge pipeline.
agent_relevance: When our agent reads a case, the weak step is deciding what the case actually shows (controls, alternatives). Code should force an explicit control/alternative slot.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench, contamination analysis (section 5.4, App. E)
finding: Compared tasks published before vs after each model's knowledge cutoff, stratified by difficulty. No consistent pre-cutoff advantage. Authors call it absence of a strong signal, not proof of absence.
numbers: Hard tasks scored higher post-cutoff: o4-mini 15.4 to 24.8, gpt-5 22.6 to 31.0. Medium: o4-mini 31.9 to 33.6, gpt-5 44.5 to 23.1. Easy o4-mini 58.9 to 42.1.
limits: Cutoff dates approximate, small per-cell samples. Constrained rediscovery (must run code) gives structural protection.
agent_relevance: For case-as-evidence: a famous case may be recalled rather than reasoned. Prefer tasks where the answer must come from running something.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench (ICML 2025)
finding: Famous textbook equations (Feynman set) are partly memorised by LLMs. Rewriting them into unusual forms (LSR-Transform) or making synthetic ones (LSR-Synth) drops accuracy sharply. Error curves on Feynman problems drop at once, which looks like recall.
numbers: 239 problems (111 LSR-Transform, rest LSR-Synth over chemistry, biology, physics, materials). Best system: symbolic accuracy 31.53% on LSR-Transform (GPT-4o-mini, LLM-SR), 28.1% best on LSR-Synth. Direct prompting without data: 7.21% (GPT-4o-mini), 3.61% (Llama-3.1-8B) on LSR-Transform. GPT-4o vs human agreement on symbolic match 94.6%.
limits: Transformed forms are still known physics in disguise. Small models used as backbone in most rows.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a well-known historical case is a weak test: the model may recite it. Disguise or alter cases (rename, change units, change form) before using them as evidence.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with LLMs
finding: Treats equations as programs. LLM proposes skeletons from domain priors, data fits parameters, evolutionary search keeps the best. Beats symbolic regression baselines, most clearly out of domain. Authors report that on Feynman problems models hit the answer in under 20 iterations, which they read as recitation, so they built novel benchmarks.
numbers: Four benchmark problems (physics, biology). Exact table values not re-extracted this session.
limits: Authors' own benchmarks; recitation claim is inference from fast convergence.
agent_relevance: A model-proposes, data-checks loop (code scores the fit on held-out OOD data) is the working form of 'test the theory on a case'. Fits G3: pass must be on data not fitted to.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld (NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks)
finding: Simulated text world with 120 discovery tasks (8 topics, 3 difficulty levels). Baseline agents do badly. Human scientists do far better.
numbers: Best discovery agent (ReAct) completed 38% of Easy and 18% of Challenge tasks. Best at finding the explanation (Hypothesizer) found 34% of gold knowledge on Easy, 8% on Challenge. Humans (up to 11 per task, 16 tasks): 66% completion, 55% knowledge. Agents are 60%+ on unit-test sub-skills.
limits: Simulated worlds with parametric variations, not real history.
agent_relevance: Agents handle single steps but fail to chain hypothesis, experiment, and explanation. Scaffold must carry the chain, with code checking the explanation was actually found.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench
finding: Tasks derived by hand from published papers' discovery workflows. Best system scores only 25%. Failures cluster in complex statistics and domain-specific workflows.
numbers: 264 real tasks over 6 domains, 903 synthetic tasks. Best agent peaks at 25%. By workflow: correlation analysis 55%, data selection 18%, summary statistics 18%, spatial analysis 0%, pollen dating 0%, ecological modeling 0%. By domain: biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%. Replicating a paper's analysis took up to 90 person-hours per dataset, about 30% not reproducible.
limits: A sentence on domain knowledge hints reads reversed in the extracted text (9.9% vs 17.5%); not trusted here.
agent_relevance: Reproducing a published case from data is itself costly and often fails; a case's reported result cannot be assumed re-derivable.

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench (ICLR 2025)
finding: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed papers, validated by nine experts. Best agent solves about a third. Expert-provided knowledge adds a little. More inference compute helps.
numbers: Best agent 32.4% unaided, 34.3% with expert knowledge (three attempts each). OpenAI o1 variant reaches 42.2%. Two contamination mitigations used (modified datasets, test-set protection).
limits: Data-driven tasks only; success is program-output match.
agent_relevance: Published-paper tasks are a usable case source only if contamination is handled; expert hints gave only +1.9 points.

source: Golchin and Surdeanu (2024) Time Travel in LLMs: Tracing Data Contamination (ICLR 2024)
finding: A guided prompt (dataset name plus start of an instance) makes the model complete the rest. If completions match references more than with a generic prompt, the data was seen in training. Detects contamination at 92-100% agreement with human experts.
numbers: Seven datasets, train and test partitions. GPT-4 found contaminated with AG News, WNLI and XSum.
limits: Needs dataset names and instance text; tests verbatim recall, not paraphrased knowledge.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-run check: before using a case, ask the model to continue its opening text. If it can, mark the case as recalled, not independent evidence.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Large Language Models for Automated Open-domain Scientific Hypotheses Discovery (MOOSE)
finding: Dataset of 50 social-science papers published after January 2023 so that targets postdate the models. A multi-module LLM framework with three feedback loops (present, past, future) raises validity, novelty and helpfulness over baselines on a 5-point GPT-4 scale. Experts also rate some outputs novel and valid.
numbers: Adding present-feedback rounds raised validness and novelty steadily; helpfulness peaked at 3 rounds. Exact table means not re-extracted.
limits: GPT-4 as judge, which G8 warns about. Social science only.
agent_relevance: Date-split case selection (only cases after the cutoff) is a cheap contamination guard. Use code-run checks instead of a model judge.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Case-based reasoning inside an agent loop. A growing case bank stores (state, action, reward) trajectories. A learned policy retrieves cases to guide the planner. No weight updates. Gains concentrate out of distribution.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% Pass@3, test 79.40%. DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM. Case memory adds 4.7 to 9.6 points on OOD tasks. Retrieved cases K=0 to 4: average F1 59.9 to 64.5, PM 72.2 to 78.5; K=8,16,32 flat or slightly lower (PM 78.2, 78.1, 78.1). Musique PM 43.8 to 52.1.
limits: Planner gpt-4.1, executor o4-mini/o3. Cases are the agent's own past trajectories, not external history.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that retrieving a few (about 4) past cases helps and more does not. Cap retrieved cases at about 4.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI 2024)
finding: Agent collects trajectories, extracts natural-language insights from success/failure pairs, and retrieves successful trajectories at test time. Insight extraction and case recall help in different tasks. Insights transfer across tasks.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38% (score 0.675 vs 0.67). Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: ExpeL transfer reaches 70% (table columns garbled in extraction; baselines roughly 58-65%). Matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% vs 39%).
limits: Small benchmarks; exact baseline cells in the transfer table uncertain.
agent_relevance: Abstracting a lesson from cases (induction) and recalling a concrete case (analogy) are separate gains; do both and keep the abstracted lesson tied to the cases it came from.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) Case-Based Reasoning with Language Models for Classification of Logical Fallacies (IJCAI)
finding: Retrieve similar past cases and adapt them. Gains of 2.5 to 6 F1 in domain and up to 8 out of domain over vanilla LMs. One retrieved case is best; more cases hurt because the model is distracted. Retrieved case labels matched the truth only 27.7% of the time, so cases help indirectly, not by label copying.
numbers: Case representation changes F1 by 6 to 8 points in domain and 4 to 8 out of domain. Counterargument enrichment gave the largest boost. 10% of the case database was enough for most of the gain.
limits: Small encoder LMs (ELECTRA, RoBERTa), classification task, not generative agents.
agent_relevance: Case value comes from how the case is represented (with counterarguments and goals), not from similarity alone. Keep few cases, and add the counter-case.

source: Hla (2026) Machina Mirabilis: GPT-1900
finding: 3.3B model trained from scratch on about 22B tokens of pre-1900 text, with midtraining on 2,600 physics texts (290M tokens), then asked to reason about Planck, photoelectric effect, relativity thought experiments. Sometimes gives near-right ideas. Author says unclear it has any real intuition.
numbers: CORE score by cutoff: pre-1900 0.1400, pre-1905 0.1632, pre-1964 0.1897, FineWeb-Edu 0.2602. No accuracy numbers on physics tests ('vibes based'). A translator's foreword naming Einstein was found late; later stages used modern LLM outputs (instruction data, Sonnet 4 as RL judge).
limits: Blog, not peer reviewed. Informal evaluation, leakage not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: A direct 'could the model have found it at the time' test of historical cases. Result: weak and unquantified; leakage is the main threat to any such test.

source: Luo et al. (2026) A Language Model from 1913: TypewriterLM
finding: 7.24B model pretrained on a 54B-token pre-1913 corpus with leakage filtering and vocabulary-constrained instruction tuning. HISTORY-EVENT benchmark of 2,344 events measures correctness before cutoff and leakage after.
numbers: Post-cutoff leakage near zero (strict 0.0-0.1%, relaxed 0.0-0.9%) across history models, but pre-cutoff factual correctness is also low (TypewriterLM base strict 0.2%, relaxed 1.2%; GPT-1900 sft strict 34.5%, relaxed 53.3%). ARC-E / ARC-C / HellaSwag: TypewriterLM 43.3/27.9/36.1; GPT-1900 base 36.7/23.9/32.3; Talkie-1930 55.8/35.6/49.8; Qwen3-4B 77.4/51.6/65.9.
limits: General competence is well below modern models, so no strong claim about rediscovery. Also reports earlier 1.3B model with a 1930 cutoff that named the 1936 US president.
agent_relevance: Period-restricted models are the cleanest contamination control for historical case tests, but they are much weaker, so a failure there says little about method.

source: Simons, Zichert and Wuthrich (2025) LLMs for History, Philosophy, and Sociology of Science
finding: Reviews how LLMs are used in HPSS and gives four lessons: model choice has interpretive trade-offs; LLM literacy is needed; HPSS must build its own benchmarks and corpora; LLMs should augment, not replace, interpretive methods.
numbers: No benchmark numbers; conceptual review.
limits: Position paper. No measured LLM results on case-study method.
agent_relevance: Confirms that no standard HPS benchmark exists, so any case-use rules we write are unvalidated and must be tested by us.

source: Zichert and Simons (2026) Computational conceptual history of scientific concepts: from early digital methods to LLMs
finding: Says LLM evaluation in HPSS has no single standard metric; triangulation of several quantitative lenses plus qualitative validation is the default. Embedding results can reflect corpus artefacts (genre, volume) rather than concept change.
numbers: None (review).
quote: triangulation will remain the default evaluation strategy
limits: Covers conceptual history, not theory-choice or case-evidence use.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: no single case or single metric settles a claim; require agreement across independent lenses.

source: Mialon, Shojaee and others; Lu et al. (2024) AI Scientist; Schmidgall (2025) Agent Laboratory (as cited in FIRE-Bench)
finding: FIRE-Bench notes end-to-end AI scientist systems rely on LLM judging as a proxy for expert review and have no objective ground truth. It proposes rediscovery of a known result as the objective alternative.
numbers: Judge validation: claim extraction/match pipeline precision 0.95, recall 0.86, F1 0.89.
limits: Description taken from the FIRE-Bench related-work and method text only.
agent_relevance: Rediscovery of a known case is the best-available objective test of a thinking scaffold, if contamination is controlled.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Processes (BACON and successors)
finding: Older AI systems (BACON, DALTON, GLAUBER, STAHL) were built to re-derive historical laws (Kepler's third law, Ohm's law, gas laws, chemical theory) from historical data. They showed rules like 'look for constant ratios' can rebuild past discoveries.
numbers: Not read this session. Known only from general knowledge; not verified.
limits: Data given in cleaned form; heuristic set tuned to the cases (the classic fitting risk).
agent_relevance: Same trap as case studies: the rebuilt discovery may be tuned to the case. Use as a model of 'case as testbed for a method'. LLM-SRBench is its modern relative.

source: Kolodner (1993) Case-Based Reasoning; Schank (1982) Dynamic Memory
finding: Classic case-based reasoning cycle: retrieve, reuse, revise, retain. Ancestor of Memento and ExpeL case banks.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Pre-LLM; claims here from general knowledge.
agent_relevance: The cycle matches our loop: revise step must use real output (G2), retain only verified cases.

source: Sauer and Scholl (eds.) (2016) The Philosophy of Historical Case Studies
finding: Philosophers debate whether historical cases can be evidence for theories of method (selection bias, theory-ladenness, the problem of too few cases). No LLM content.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; title and scope only.
agent_relevance: Source of the human-side rules (pre-register what the case should show, report cases that fail) that LLM studies above do not test.

source: Cross-reading: contamination controls across the benchmarks above
finding: Five different guards appear in the opened papers: alter the form (LSR-Transform), synthesise new problems (LSR-Synth, LLM-SR), date-split to post-cutoff papers (MOOSE, FIRE-Bench analysis), modify data and protect the test set (ScienceAgentBench), and a model with a historical cutoff (GPT-1900, TypewriterLM).
numbers: Effect of alteration: LSR-Transform best symbolic accuracy 31.5% vs far higher on the original Feynman set per the paper's figure (exact Feynman figure not re-extracted).
limits: None of the guards is proven complete; FIRE-Bench found no consistent cutoff effect, so date-splits may be weak or noisy.
agent_relevance: Our case library should carry a contamination field per case: altered, synthetic, post-cutoff, or recalled.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento, ablation across iterations
finding: Without the case bank, performance still rises over five iterations by repeated tries. The case bank is compared against that baseline on DeepResearcher.
numbers: Memento without case-based reasoning: 78.65, 80.93, 82.62, 83.53, 84.47 over iterations 1-5 (PM). Case-based rows were not re-extracted.
limits: Gap to the case-based rows not read; do not quote a gain from this line.
agent_relevance: Any case-memory gain must be measured against repeated plain attempts at equal tokens (G7).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench, method comparison
finding: Methods that check candidates against data beat direct prompting by large factors. Different strategies win on different domains (LaSR better symbolic accuracy in materials, LLM-SR better numeric precision).
numbers: LSR-Transform symbolic accuracy: direct prompting 3.61 (Llama-3.1-8B), 2.10 (GPT-3.5), 7.21 (GPT-4o-mini); LLM-SR 30.63, 10.81, 31.53 respectively.
limits: Same benchmark authors built it; small LLM backbones.
agent_relevance: Gap of about 4x between recall-only and data-checked answers shows value of executing the check.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld, unit tests
finding: On ten small unit-test tasks agents do moderately, on the full discovery tasks poorly. So the failure is composition of steps, not individual skills.
numbers: Unit-test averages around 0.66-0.77 completion across three agents versus 0.18-0.38 on Easy/Normal full tasks.
limits: Table columns partly garbled in extraction; ranges are approximate.
agent_relevance: Argues for a state machine where code sequences the steps and the model fills one slot at a time.

source: Luo et al. (2026) TypewriterLM, related-work report on leakage
finding: Reports that a 1.3B model with a 1930 cutoff still named the US president in 1936, and notes the pre-1900 GPT-1900 may carry similar leaks. Their pipeline filters at both corpus and instruction-tuning stages.
numbers: Leakage on HISTORY-EVENT post-cutoff: strict 0.0 to 0.1%, relaxed up to 0.9% across listed models.
limits: Second-hand report of the other model's leak.
agent_relevance: Even deliberately period-limited models leak; a 'blind' case test needs a measured leakage rate.

source: Zichert and Simons (2026); Simons et al. (2025), on benchmarks for HPSS
finding: Both papers say HPSS has no widely accepted evaluation datasets, rarely has stable ground truth, and must build its own corpora. I found no study testing LLMs on Kuhn, Lakatos, or case-study method per se in six web searches and several arXiv fetches (two search tools were rate-limited).
numbers: Zero direct studies found. Search coverage: 5 WebSearch calls, arXiv/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar APIs returned 429.
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: The method-of-cases question for LLMs is open; our own tests (altered cases, held-out cases) are the evidence we will have.
